title: Rogers Communications Canada Nationwide Network Outage (July 2022)

severity.usersAffected: ~12 million subscribers nationwide; 911 and Interac payment networks down
severity.impactUsd: Regulator-ordered credits + reputational cost; exact figure not consolidated

brief: A maintenance change to Rogers' core IP network removed a routing filter, flooding the routers and collapsing the entire national network — taking mobile, internet, 911 emergency calling and Interac payments offline across Canada for roughly 15 hours and affecting about 12 million subscribers.

magnitude.note: National telecom/IP core collapse: mobile, internet, 911, and Interac payments down for ~26 h (CRTC window) for ~12M subscribers — sub-scores ESTIMATED from public impact reporting, pending deep research.

rootCause:
The direct trigger was a change-management action, not a physical ignition: during the sixth phase of a seven-phase upgrade to Rogers' core IP network, staff removed the Access Control List (ACL) policy filter from the configuration of the distribution routers. The CRTC-commissioned independent (Xona) assessment states "Rogers staff removed the Access Control List policy filter from the configuration of the distribution routers," and quantifies the result: about 10,000 routes are advertised into the core with the filter present, but "when this policy filter was removed, a single distribution router released over 900,000 route data into the core routers." That flood exceeded processing capacity and "the core network routers crashed within minutes from the time the policy filter was removed" — a control-plane/route-table congestive collapse. No fire, combustion, or chemistry was involved; the "ignition source" analog is the ACL deletion and the "fuel" is the uncontrolled route-table injection that saturated the core routers.

The specific equipment implicated was the Rogers IP-core routing tier — distribution routers feeding the core network routers. Critically, the router vendor, model, firmware version, and hardware age are NOT publicly disclosed; they were not identified in the public CRTC/Xona assessment or Rogers' CRTC filings, so make/model/age cannot be traced to a source and are recorded here as unknown.

The latent root causes are design, redundancy, and maintenance/testing lapses that turned a single foreseeable misconfiguration into a national collapse. Design: the converged architecture ran wireless and wireline over one shared IP core, so per the CRTC "the scope of the outage was extreme in that it resulted in a catastrophic loss of all services." Overload protection: "the Rogers core network routers were not configured with such overload protection mechanisms," so nothing rejected the flood. Management redundancy: Rogers "did not provision its network operation centre and other critical remote infrastructure sites with redundant connectivity from alternative service providers," and the outage severed internal access including "the company's VPN to its core network nodes," blinding responders. Maintenance/testing: the change was pushed to production without adequate staged lab validation — the CRTC recommended Rogers "ensure wide coverage and rigor in testing configuration changes" — with no rollback containment, fault isolation, or inter-operator emergency-roaming failover for 9-1-1.
technicalDeepDive:
The failure was a route-table congestive collapse propagating through a converged IP core. In normal operation Rogers' distribution routers passed a filtered, bounded set of routes into the core — the CRTC/Xona assessment states "about 10,000 routes are advertised into the core router when the Access Control List policy filter is present on the distribution router" — with the ACL filter acting as the guardrail that constrained what routing information could enter the core. Phase six of a seven-phase core upgrade removed that ACL filter from the distribution-router configuration. Rogers told the CRTC that "the deletion of a routing filter on its distribution routers caused all possible routes to the internet to pass through the routers, exceeding the capacity of the routers on its core network." The assessment quantifies one distribution router alone injecting "over 900,000 route data into the core routers," and "the core network routers crashed within minutes from the time the policy filter was removed."

Because the crashed core carried Rogers' external reachability, the ASN's global advertisements collapsed with it. Cloudflare's external BGP telemetry captured the signature from outside the network: "there was a clear spike in BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) updates after 08:15, reaching its peak at 08:45," and "at 08:45 there was a withdrawal of prefixes from Rogers ASN" (times UTC; 08:45 UTC = 04:45 EDT). That prefix withdrawal is why the outage was total and instantaneous from the public Internet's perspective — Rogers effectively disappeared from the global routing table. Cloudflare assessed the pattern as "likely to be an internal error, not a cyber attack."

Two architectural facts made a control-plane bug catastrophic rather than contained. First, convergence: wireless and wireline shared one IP core, so there was no partition to absorb the fault — mobile, home Internet, enterprise, 9-1-1, and Interac dropped simultaneously ("a catastrophic loss of all services"). Second, no independent management path: once the core crashed, Rogers employees lost "internal access to systems such as the company's VPN to its core network nodes, hampering the ability of the company's employees to mobilize a team and identify the issue." Recovery therefore could not be a simple rollback; responders first had to regain management reach, isolate the flooding distribution routers, purge the injected routing state, and rebuild the core route tables and services in stages. Cloudflare's telemetry shows the halting recovery: an advertisement attempt "at 14:30," "another round of withdraws at around 15:45" (a setback), "partial recovery of traffic from the Rogers network, mostly after 00:15 UTC" on 9 July, and "around 76% of the previous day traffic at the same time" by 08:40 UTC on 9 July — with Cloudflare still seeing "frequent BGP announcement and withdrawals" (core "flapping" not fully resolved), consistent with the CRTC dating full restoration to 07:00 EDT on 9 July.

sequenceOfEvents.event: During phase six of a seven-phase core IP-network upgrade, Rogers staff remove the Access Control List (ACL) policy filter from the distribution routers' configuration.
With the filter gone, all possible Internet routes pass into the core; a single distribution router releases over 900,000 route entries into the core routers versus ~10,000 normally.
The route flood exceeds the core routers' processing capacity; the core network routers crash within minutes of the filter's removal.

External BGP telemetry (Cloudflare) records a spike in BGP updates after 08:15 UTC, peaking at 08:45 UTC, with a withdrawal of prefixes from the Rogers ASN — Rogers vanishes from the global routing table.
Rogers is internally blind: the outage severs internal access to systems including the VPN to core network nodes, hampering employees' ability to mobilize a team and identify the issue.
Nationwide outage onset — more than 12 million customers lose wireless and wireline services (mobile, home Internet, corporate and institutional).

9-1-1 access from Rogers mobile phones is unavailable; a Hamilton man reportedly could not call 911 as his sister was dying, though it is unclear whether the death could have been avoided had 911 contact been possible.
Interac is taken offline by the outage, preventing businesses nationwide from accepting debit-card transactions even on other ISPs; some stores temporarily close.

No suppression analog activates: core routers had no overload protection and the converged architecture had no automatic partition, so nothing contained the flood — a catastrophic loss of all services.

Recovery cannot be a simple rollback; because the VPN to core nodes is lost, responders must regain management reach, then isolate the flooding distribution routers, purge bad routing state, and rebuild core route tables in stages.
Cloudflare observes a first attempt to re-advertise Rogers prefixes as the staged rebuild begins.
'Another round of withdraws at around 15:45' — Rogers prefixes are withdrawn again, a recovery setback amid core-network flapping.
Partial recovery of traffic from the Rogers network, mostly after 00:15 UTC, as services are rebuilt in stages.
Traffic reaches around 76% of the previous day's level at the same time, though frequent BGP announcements/withdrawals show the core flapping issue is not yet fully resolved.
CRTC dates full restoration; the outage window runs 04:58 EDT 8 July to 07:00 EDT 9 July (approximately 26 hours).
Minister Champagne sets a 60-day deadline for carriers to agree mutual assistance and emergency roaming; Rogers pledges $261 million to physically separate its wireless and wireline networks.

contributingFactors: Maintenance/change-control lapse: the ACL policy filter was removed from distribution-router configuration during phase six of a seven-phase core upgrade, with no safeguard against the resulting route flood (CRTC/Xona; Rogers' CRTC letter via Wikipedia).

Inadequate pre-deployment testing: the change reached production without adequate staged lab validation; the CRTC recommended Rogers 'ensure wide coverage and rigor in testing configuration changes' (CRTC/Xona).

No overload protection on core routers: 'the Rogers core network routers were not configured with such overload protection mechanisms,' so >900,000 routes (vs ~10,000 normal) crashed the core within minutes (CRTC/Xona).

Converged single-core architecture: wireless and wireline shared one IP core, so the outage 'resulted in a catastrophic loss of all services' — one change felled mobile, wireline, and 9-1-1 together (CRTC/Xona).

No independent management path: Rogers lacked redundant NOC/site connectivity from alternative providers, and the outage severed internal access including 'the company's VPN to its core network nodes,' delaying responders (CRTC/Xona; Rogers' CRTC letter via Wikipedia).

No inter-carrier emergency-roaming failover: Rogers mobile users had no 9-1-1 fallback during the outage, prompting the post-incident emergency-roaming mandate (CRTC/Xona; Champagne undertakings via Wikipedia).

coe.action: Physically separate wireless and wireline core networks ($261M pledge) so one fault cannot collapse all services
Implement router overload protection (max-prefix / route limits / control-plane policing) on core routers
Provision independent/out-of-band management and redundant NOC connectivity from alternative providers
Strengthen configuration-change control with wide-coverage, rigorous pre-deployment lab testing and staged validation
coe.owner: Rogers Communications (change management), per CRTC recommendation

coe.action: Agree inter-carrier mutual-assistance and emergency-roaming arrangements within 60 days
coe.owner: All Canadian telecom providers, mandated by Minister Champagne / ISED

coe.action: Establish and regularly test 9-1-1 emergency-roaming failover across carriers

lessonsLearnt: A single removed guardrail in a converged core is a national single point of failure: removing one ACL filter injected over 900,000 routes and crashed the core within minutes, taking mobile, wireline, 9-1-1, and Interac down together (CRTC/Xona).

The management plane must survive the data plane it manages: because the VPN to core nodes rode the failed network, Rogers was blinded and could not quickly mobilize or roll back — independent, out-of-band access is not optional (CRTC/Xona; Rogers' CRTC letter).
Overload protection must be assumed-on, not assumed-safe: core routers with no route-limit safeguard forwarded themselves to death when a foreseeable misconfiguration occurred (CRTC/Xona).

Change control needs rigorous staged lab validation and tested rollback: pushing an unfiltered configuration into production during phase six of a live seven-phase upgrade converted a routine change into a ~26-hour national outage (CRTC/Xona; Rogers' CRTC letter).

Critical-infrastructure dependencies are systemic: Interac and 9-1-1 riding on one carrier pushed the failure into nationwide debit payments and emergency calling, well beyond Rogers' own subscribers (Wikipedia).

Vendor detail can be a documented gap: the failed routers' make, model, firmware, and age were never publicly disclosed, so this analysis records them as unknown rather than inventing them (CRTC/Xona; public filings).
improvements: Design: Physically separate the wireless and wireline core networks so a single fault cannot collapse all services simultaneously — Rogers pledged $261 million toward this separation (Wikipedia; CRTC/Xona rationale).

Design: Implement router overload-protection mechanisms (max-prefix / route limits / control-plane policing) on core routers so a route flood is rejected rather than allowed to crash the control plane (CRTC/Xona).

Design: Provide a management path physically independent of the data network, plus redundant NOC/site connectivity from alternative service providers, so responders retain access even when the core fails (CRTC/Xona).

Maintenance: Strengthen configuration-change control with rigorous, wide-coverage pre-deployment lab testing and staged validation of every core-router change, with tested rollback before production rollout (CRTC/Xona).

Process: Establish an inter-carrier framework for mutual assistance, emergency roaming for rivals' affected customers, and coordinated public communication, on the 60-day deadline set by Minister Champagne (Wikipedia; CRTC/Xona).
Safety: Guarantee 9-1-1 continuity via inter-operator emergency-roaming failover, tested regularly, so mobile emergency calling survives a single carrier's core outage (CRTC/Xona; Wikipedia).

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: No fire — a congestive control-plane collapse
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: This was not a physical or thermal event; it was a routing/control-plane failure. The 'ignition' analog is the deletion of the ACL policy filter on the distribution routers, and the 'fuel' is the uncontrolled injection of routing state into the core. With the filter present, roughly 10,000 routes reached the core; with it gone, a single distribution router pushed 'over 900,000 route data into the core routers,' exceeding processing capacity and crashing the core 'within minutes.' The mechanism is specific and vendor-agnostic: route-table saturation of the control plane, not any hardware defect.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Latent causes: convergence, no overload protection, no independent management
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Three latent conditions turned a foreseeable misconfiguration into a national outage. Convergence put wireless and wireline on one IP core, so the CRTC found the fault 'resulted in a catastrophic loss of all services' with no partition to contain it. Core routers had no overload protection ('were not configured with such overload protection mechanisms'), so nothing rejected the flood. And the management path was not independent — Rogers lacked redundant NOC connectivity and lost 'the company's VPN to its core network nodes,' blinding responders and preventing a quick rollback.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: External signature and staged recovery
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Cloudflare's BGP telemetry provides an independent, timestamped view: a spike in BGP updates 'after 08:15, reaching its peak at 08:45,' then 'a withdrawal of prefixes from Rogers ASN' (UTC) — Rogers vanishing from the global table. Recovery was halting: a re-advertisement attempt at 14:30 UTC, 'another round of withdraws at around 15:45,' partial traffic 'mostly after 00:15 UTC,' and about 76% of prior-day traffic by 08:40 UTC on 9 July, with continued flapping. This matches the CRTC's ~26-hour window (04:58 EDT 8 Jul to 07:00 EDT 9 Jul) and the need to isolate routers, purge state, and rebuild in stages.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Systemic impact and regulatory response
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Because critical services rode Rogers' single core, the blast radius exceeded its own subscribers: more than 12 million customers lost service, Interac debit went offline 'nationwide,' and 9-1-1 was unavailable from Rogers mobile — with a reported Hamilton death whose avoidability is unclear. The response was structural: Rogers pledged $261 million to physically separate wireless and wireline, and Minister Champagne gave carriers 60 days to agree mutual assistance and emergency roaming, with the CRTC/Xona assessment recommending overload protection, independent management, and rigorous change testing.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Disclosed gaps
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The router vendor, model, firmware version, and hardware age are not established by any public source and are recorded as unknown rather than inferred. The exact wall-clock time of the ACL removal is not published; it is bounded only as shortly before the 04:58 EDT onset and consistent with Cloudflare's ~08:15-08:45 UTC BGP activity. The 'substantial restoration within ~15-19 hours' figure from the source draft is unsupported and was removed; the defensible measure is the ~26-hour outage window and the 76%-by-08:40-UTC recovery point.

fmea.scope: Rogers' national IP core: the change process for the seven-phase core upgrade, the ACL policy filter on the distribution routers, core-router overload protection, the converged wireless/wireline core, the management path to core nodes, staged recovery, 9-1-1 continuity and the third-party services (Interac) that rode the network. Analysed retrospectively from the CRTC-commissioned independent (Xona) assessment, Rogers' letter to the CRTC as relayed by Wikipedia, and Cloudflare BGP telemetry. The router vendor, model, firmware and age are not public and are not used. Only one action, the $261M wireless/wireline separation, is recorded as a Rogers commitment; the others are CRTC/Xona directions or recommendations, or a ministerial mandate, with completion not recorded, so those modes carry no revised score.

modes.function: Apply configuration changes to distribution routers without altering what routing state reaches the core
modes.failureMode: The ACL policy filter is removed from the distribution routers' configuration, letting all possible Internet routes into the core
modes.effect: A single distribution router releases over 900,000 routes into the core against about 10,000 normally; the core crashes within minutes and more than 12 million customers lose wireless and wireline service
modes.cause: Change pushed to production without adequate staged lab validation and with no safeguard against the resulting route flood
modes.prevention: A phased upgrade plan; no recorded pre-deployment test of this change
modes.detection: None inside Rogers before impact; Cloudflare saw a BGP update spike from 08:15 UTC and Rogers prefixes withdrawn at 08:45 UTC

rationale.S: Provider-wide outage of every service a national carrier runs, with no workaround for its customers: the rubric's 9. The hazard to people through 9-1-1 is scored separately in FM-06.
rationale.O: A configuration change in a planned upgrade is routine work, and deleting a filter is a foreseeable slip that nothing in the process guarded: 'occasional'.
rationale.D: No test or check caught the change before it took effect, and Rogers' own access was cut by the outage; the failure is visible in the record through external BGP telemetry and customer loss.

evidence.quote: a single distribution router released over 900,000 route data into the core routers

actions.text: Strengthen configuration-change control with wide-coverage, rigorous pre-deployment lab testing and staged validation (recommended by CRTC/Xona; completion not recorded)

playbook.do: Lab-test the exact phase-six configuration, including the filter removal, and require a peer sign-off before it reaches production
Apply the change to one distribution router first and watch its route count against the ~10,000 norm before the next
Alarm the NOC when a distribution router advertises more routes to the core than a set ceiling, well under 900,000
Stop the upgrade on any alarm and order the change owner to restore the filter on the router in question
Reapply the ACL policy filter on the distribution routers once management access is back

modes.function: Reject or limit an excessive route injection instead of processing it to failure
modes.failureMode: Core routers accept the route flood and crash within minutes
modes.effect: The core control plane collapses and Rogers' ASN disappears from the global routing table
modes.cause: Core routers 'were not configured with such overload protection mechanisms' (max-prefix, route limits, control-plane policing)

rationale.S: This is the step that turned a filter deletion into a national collapse, so it carries the same severity as FM-01.
rationale.O: The missing protection is a standing condition, but it only fails when an unbounded route injection arrives, which needs a change like FM-01 first: 'infrequent'. Kept below FM-01 so the event is not counted twice at full weight.
rationale.D: Nothing recorded flagged the route-table growth before the crash 'within minutes'; it was seen after impact.

evidence.quote: the Rogers core network routers were not configured with such overload protection mechanisms

actions.text: Implement router overload protection (max-prefix, route limits, control-plane policing) on core routers (directed by CRTC/Xona findings; completion not recorded)

playbook.do: Configure max-prefix limits and control-plane policing on every core router
Alert on core-router CPU and route-table growth rate, not only on link loss
Shut the BGP sessions from the flooding distribution router so the core stops receiving the routes
Declare a national incident and make clearing the flooding distribution routers the first step
Reboot the crashed core routers only once the flood source is isolated

modes.cause: No partition between wireless and wireline in the core architecture
modes.detection: None recorded; the shared fate showed itself at onset through loss of all services

rationale.S: Loss of all of a national carrier's services at once is the rubric's 9.
rationale.O: Needs a core-wide fault first, which is infrequent.
rationale.D: No control contained or flagged the shared fate; it was learned through the outage itself.

actions.text: Physically separate wireless and wireline core networks ($261M pledge) so one fault cannot collapse all services
Physically separate the wireless and wireline core networks

modes.revisedRationale: With separate cores, a fault of this kind would take down one service family rather than both (S 9→8; still a full outage of a major service for hours). O and D are unchanged because separation does not stop the triggering fault or detect it. Rogers' pledge is recorded as committed post-incident, not as completed, so the reduction is a claim about the action, not a confirmed outcome.

playbook.do: Fund and finish the physical split of the wireless and wireline cores
Track per-service health (mobile, home internet, 9-1-1 path) separately so a shared-core fault is seen as one event
Order the unaffected service family to be cut off from the failing core if the split exists
Say at once that mobile, internet and 9-1-1 are all down, rather than service by service
Restore the services that carry 9-1-1 first, then mobile, then fixed lines

modes.item: Management path to core nodes and NOC connectivity
modes.function: Keep responders able to reach, diagnose and roll back core equipment while the core is down
modes.failureMode: The management VPN to core nodes rides the failed network, so responders lose access
modes.effect: Employees cannot quickly mobilise a team or identify the issue; recovery cannot be a simple rollback and must first regain management reach
modes.cause: No management path independent of the data network; NOC and critical remote sites lacked redundant connectivity from alternative providers

rationale.S: This mode sets how long the outage lasted rather than whether it happened; many hours of full outage of a major service is the rubric's 8.
rationale.O: A standing dependency exercised whenever the core fails, weakly guarded: 'occasional'.
rationale.D: No test of management access under a core failure is recorded; the dependency surfaced when responders were locked out.

evidence.quote: did not provision its network operation centre and other critical remote infrastructure sites with redundant connectivity from alternative service providers

actions.text: Provision independent out-of-band management and redundant NOC connectivity from alternative providers (directed by CRTC/Xona findings; completion not recorded)

playbook.do: Build a management path on a separate provider and redundant NOC links, independent of the Rogers data network
Test out-of-band access to core nodes monthly with the main network deliberately disabled
Switch the response team to the out-of-band path and phones, since the VPN to core nodes is gone
Mobilise engineers on site to the core nodes when remote access fails
Regain management reach before touching the routers, then roll back the filter change

modes.function: Rebuild the core route tables and services quickly and stably after a collapse

modes.cause: No rollback containment or fault isolation for this change; responders had to isolate the flooding routers, purge routing state and rebuild in stages

rationale.S: It stretches the outage, but FM-04 already carries the duration at 8, so this mode is scored one step lower to avoid counting the same hours twice at full weight.
rationale.O: Present whenever a core-wide collapse needs rebuilding, with no recorded rehearsed rollback: between 'infrequent' and 'occasional'.
rationale.D: No rehearsal is recorded that would reveal recovery time or flapping before an incident; the setbacks were seen in external BGP telemetry as they happened.

evidence.quote: at 08:45 there was a withdrawal of prefixes from Rogers ASN

actions.text: Staged validation of every core-router change with tested rollback before production rollout (analyst/CRTC recommendation; no status)

playbook.do: Write and rehearse a rollback for each phase of the core upgrade, with timings
Watch BGP announcements and withdrawals during the rebuild and flag flapping as a setback
Re-advertise prefixes in small groups and pause when a group flaps, as the 15:45 UTC withdrawal showed
Set fixed checkpoints for the rebuild and report restored traffic percentage at each
Purge bad routing state and rebuild core route tables in stages until traffic is stable

modes.function: Keep emergency calling available when one carrier's core fails
modes.failureMode: Rogers mobile users cannot reach 9-1-1, with no inter-carrier emergency-roaming fallback

rationale.S: Loss of emergency calling is a hazard to people, the rubric's 10, and the dossier records at least one reported death during the outage, with avoidability unclear.
rationale.O: Needs a carrier-wide core failure first, which is infrequent.
rationale.D: No fallback existed to detect or bridge the loss; it was found by people who could not get through.
